name: Nikhil Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nikhil, 27, and I'm a senior operator at an iron ore mine out in the desert, about an hour's drive from town. Half our haul trucks already drive themselves, and I'm the field lead in the zone where people and driverless trucks share the roads. I share a house in town with two mates from the mine, and my girlfriend Priya lives in the city, so it's a lot of weekend driving.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at half five with a pre-start meeting, then I'm in a grader or a light vehicle, keeping the haul roads right and clearing the zone when a driverless truck stops because it's seen a rock or a kangaroo. I'm on the radio to the control centre all day. I love the puzzle of it, figuring out why a truck has frozen and getting it moving again. What wears me out is the heat in summer, and the paperwork when anything goes even slightly wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use a chatbot to study for my certificate in automation, to write up incident reports faster and to check the fault codes the trucks throw. My crew think I'm a bit obsessed, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit of a letdown for me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the automation we've already got works well and it's made the pit safer, even if the hype was too big. I'd probably post something like that, and add that the tools are still useful. People at work would rib me about it for weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. My job is safe, the mine has a long life and I'd keep moving up. I'd lose a bit of the excitement about where I could go, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my automation certificate anyway and apply for a controller seat in the remote operations centre in the city, which would put me closer to Priya. I'd keep putting about a fifth of my pay into an index fund. And I'd keep using AI for the boring writing, because it already saves me an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you even in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The driving to see Priya. Four hours each way every swing off is wearing me down. That's why the city control centre job matters more to me than the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you have saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five months of expenses in the bank, plus the index fund, which is down a bit this year. Enough that I'm not scared of a gap between jobs.

say: The hype was **too big**, but the automation already in the pit **works well**.
Driverless trucks have made the **pit safer**, and he'd say so.
think: His job is **safe** and the mine has a **long life**.
He'd only lose some **excitement** about where his career could go.
do: Apply for a **controller seat** in the city operations centre, near Priya.
Keep putting a **fifth of his pay** into an index fund.
S0.quote: The automation we've already got works well and it's made the pit safer, even if the hype was too big.
fieldNote: Already works beside **driverless trucks**, so AI isn't abstract for him.
His real pressure is **distance from Priya**, not technology.
Saves and invests with **unusual discipline** for his age.

steps.text: Finish the automation certificate he's already studying
Apply for a controller seat in the city operations centre
Put a fifth of his pay into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's kind of the world I already live in at work, just more of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good, as long as the gains are shared. I'd post that we need the union to get retraining written into every agreement, because not everyone has my head for this stuff. The guys who drove trucks for twenty years deserve a real path, not a pamphlet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. More automation means more people needed to set it up, fix it and supervise it, at least for a while. My incident reports and fault checking would be done by software, which frees me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get into the commissioning team that sets up driverless fleets at new pits. I'd use the AI tools even more, to learn the control software before anyone asks me to. I'd also volunteer to run training for older drivers moving into other roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. Guilty about being excited, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old trainer Steve lost his seat when the first driverless trucks came in. I'm doing well out of the same thing that knocked him down. Steve is on the wash bay now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone has your head for this. Who would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older drivers who never touched a computer, and the ones whose English isn't strong, because all the new training is on screens. Some of them are the best operators I know.

say: Automation is good if the **gains are shared**.
The union should write **retraining** into every agreement for long-serving drivers.
think: More automation means more people to **set up and fix** it, for a while.
Software doing his **reports and fault checks** frees him up.
do: Push to join the **commissioning team** for new driverless fleets.
Learn the **control software** with AI tools before he's asked.
Volunteer to **train older drivers** moving to other roles.
S1.quote: My old trainer Steve lost his seat when the first driverless trucks came in. I'm doing well out of the same thing that knocked him down.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **career ladder**, not a threat.
**Guilt** about older colleagues sits beside his excitement.
Progressive views show up as concern for **who gets left behind**.

steps.text: Learn the driverless fleet control software using AI tools
Apply to the commissioning team for new driverless fleets
Push the union to write retraining into the next agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one is different. That actually gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer straight away, things like a basic income and taxing the companies that own the robots. I'd post about it a lot, probably too much. I'd also tell people at work not to panic, which would be a bit rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here's the thing that gets me. The control room job I'm aiming for is thinking work, and the card says that goes in 2028. My hands-on field work lasts until about 2031. So the jobs I've been climbing towards disappear before the ones I'm climbing away from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd drop the control room plan and move towards hands-on maintenance of the robots and sensors, because that lasts the extra three years. I'd keep investing, because if robots do all the work, owning a piece of the companies matters. I'd talk to Priya about moving in together to halve the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like I'd been reading the map upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell people not to panic. Are you panicking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not panicking. I've got savings, no kids and I learn fast. But I'd be worried in a way I'm not now, because there isn't a next rung in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe I'm one of the few people who keep the robots honest for a few more years. Maybe I'm out. I'd want the shares and the savings to carry me while I work it out.

say: It needs a **political answer** now: a **basic income** and taxing robot owners.
He'd tell coworkers **not to panic**, though he admits that's a bit rich.
think: The **control room job** he wants is thinking work, gone in 2028.
His **hands-on field work** lasts until about 2031.
do: Drop the control room plan and move to **robot maintenance**.
Keep **investing**, since owning part of the companies would matter.
Move in with Priya to **halve the rent**.
feel: **Unsettled**, as if he'd been reading the **map upside down**.
S2.quote: The jobs I've been climbing towards disappear before the ones I'm climbing away from.
fieldNote: He spots that the **control room** is more exposed than the pit floor.
Not panicked: **savings, no kids** and fast learning give him some control.
Turns to **owning shares** as a hedge, alongside basic income politics.

steps.text: Switch from the control room plan to robot and sensor maintenance
Keep putting a fifth of his pay into shares
Campaign online for a basic income and robot tax
Move in with Priya to halve the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gives me a bit of room to be clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if governments start now. I'd post about retraining funds and basic income trials. At work I'd be the guy telling everyone to start learning something this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'd get maybe three or four years in the commissioning team before the thinking side goes. Then a few years in hands-on robot maintenance until about 2034. After that, I honestly don't know, and that's the part I'd be chewing on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the commissioning work for two or three years and save hard, maybe up to a year of expenses. I'd get an electrical licence on the side, because fixing robots needs it. And I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a planning way. Five years feels like a long trip where you know the fuel runs low near the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya about the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we shouldn't buy a house in a mining town, and we should think about having kids somewhere with lots of different jobs. She works in hospital admin, which is thinking work, so she's more exposed than me early on. We'd both be retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone, for how this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the engineers. The governments who saw it coming and did nothing, if that's what happens. Five years is enough warning to have a plan.

say: Five years is enough to **do this properly** if governments start now.
He'd urge coworkers to start **learning something** this year.
think: He'd get three or four years in **commissioning**, then robot maintenance to **2034**.
After **2034** he honestly doesn't know what he'd do.
do: Work in **commissioning** for two or three years and save **a year** of expenses.
Get an **electrical licence** on the side.

S3.quote: Five years feels like a long trip where you know the fuel runs low near the end.
fieldNote: He maps his career **year by year** against the card's dates.
Notices his partner Priya's **admin job** is more exposed than his.

steps.text: Save a full year of expenses while in commissioning
Get an electrical licence on the side
Keep investing in shares every month
Agree with Priya not to buy in a mining town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Yeah, that I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make this a good thing for most people, if we start now. I'd be arguing for things like shorter working weeks and shared ownership. Online I'd probably sound like an optimist, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be okay. I'd have most of a career in automation before the robots match people in 2039, and by then I'd have savings, shares and maybe a house. I'd be 39 with options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the city control room after all, for five or six years, to be near Priya. Then I'd shift to robot maintenance or commissioning before 2036. I'd keep investing, and we'd probably buy a place in the city around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry about everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Everyone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My housemates, mostly. My housemate Jono drives a water cart and has never opened a laptop. In ten years he could learn something, but he won't unless someone makes him. I'd be on his case about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. What would make you wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine automates early and the city jobs go before 2036. Or if the shares crash. I know I'm guessing; nobody really knows how these things land.

say: Ten years is enough to make this **good for most people**.
He'd argue for **shorter working weeks** and shared ownership.
think: He'd have most of a **career in automation** before robots match people.
At 39 he'd have **savings, shares** and maybe a house.
do: Take the **city control room** job for five or six years.
Buy a **place in the city** with Priya around year three.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with **worry** for friends like Jono.
S4.quote: My housemate Jono drives a water cart and has never opened a laptop. In ten years he could learn something, but he won't unless someone makes him.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his worry outward, to **friends who won't adapt**.
He's honest that his plan rests on **guesses** about timing and markets.
Sounds **optimistic** and means it, a contrast with the faster pictures.

steps.text: Take a city control room job for five or six years
Buy a place in the city with Priya around year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it flips everything. The control room and the planning jobs I thought were safe go first. What would help is the mine paying for people to move into hands-on robot work early, and a government that has a basic income ready before it's needed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who already lost out. We talk about AI like it's future tense, but at my mine the first driverless trucks came years ago. There are drivers on the wash bay right now who could tell you how this feels.

headlineQuote: We talk about AI like it's future tense, but at my mine the first driverless trucks came years ago.
portrait: A 27-year-old **field lead** in the driverless haul zone of an iron ore mine, who uses AI tools every day.
Progressive and keen on technology; worried about **older drivers** who already lost their seats.
Calm in the slower pictures, where automation is a **career ladder** for him.
In AGI by 2028 he sees the **control room** jobs he wanted vanish before the hands-on ones.
Plans with **savings, shares** and an electrical licence, and admits much of it is a guess.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the planning jobs he thought were safe would go **first**.
whatWouldHelp: The mine paying for early moves into **hands-on robot work**.
A **basic income** ready before it's needed.
